## Module 8 in two minutes

Seven modules of restraint, boundaries, and things you may not ask a model to do. This one asks what all of it was for, and the answer is one sentence that is **not** the sentence your function is measured on.

> **The product is not a closed case. It is a finding that holds.**

**Cycle time and closure rate are both genuinely important** — a matter left open is a harm continuing, a complainant waiting, a respondent under a cloud. And **both score the same on the day of closure regardless of whether the finding will hold.** A matter closed fast on a record that collapses appears in your numbers as a success for one to three years, and then appears somewhere else. The metrics you are measured on are systematically blind to the thing you are for.

**What holding looks like — seven modules, one list.** A finding holds when **the rung boundaries are visible in the file**; **the conflicts are recorded as conflicts**, located and left unresolved on the page until a human resolves them in their own name; **the human resolution is attributable to a human**, so that eighteen months later the file answers *who decided this and on what basis*; **every allegation has a resolution**, including the ones recorded as unresolved with why; **the comparator question was asked before the decision** rather than after the claim; and **the authority you relied on was dated.**

Notice what the list omits: **nothing about speed, volume, or tooling.** A finding can hold in a matter that took four months and one that took eleven days. The question is whether you can tell the difference **before somebody else does.**

### What to measure instead

**This function has an unusual advantage: the benchmark exists.** Most roles on this ladder are guessing about their peers. Employee relations has an annual study with a disclosed sample — **274 US organizations of 1,000+ employees, 8.8 million employees, ±5.9 points**, vendor-sponsored and independently fielded, and silent about employers below 1,000.

**Substantiation by issue type** — harassment, discrimination, retaliation, policy breach recorded separately. **Only 32% track it**, and without that granularity a 60% aggregate can hide 75% for policy breaches and 25% for harassment. The second is the number that appears in a claim.

**Whether a required investigation process exists at all** — **38% operate without one.** The least glamorous number in the study and the most consequential, because every capability in this track sits on top of a process. **If you are in that 38%, the highest-value change available to you is not AI.**

**Time-to-first-contact rather than time-to-close** — a different instrument. One measures how fast you finish; the other measures how fast a person who raised something stops waiting in silence. It is also the one number here you can start collecting this week.

**Repeat-respondent detection** — how you learn that three separate, individually-unsubstantiated matters name the same person. The aggregate outcome hides this by design, and it is where the real exposure usually lives.

**And the one nobody measures: what share of your closed matters could withstand the comparator analysis opposing counsel would run?** You will not get a number in a quarter. Ask it about ten specific files anyway — the answer is either *most of them* or a sinking feeling, and both are information.

**One caution.** These are aggregates about organisations, not targets. **Do not turn a benchmark into a goal** — committing to reach a published rate commits you to a number rather than to accuracy.

**The honest capacity conversation, and then the bet.**

**Volumes at or near decade highs. Serious allegations more than doubled since 2021. Staffing from roughly 0.6 to 0.68 professionals per 1,000 employees.** Demand has outrun capacity and headcount will not close it — and 70% of ER teams have already experimented with or deployed AI, which means **adoption is following the pressure, not a strategy.**

> **AI in this function is not a productivity story. It is a triage story.**

A productivity story says *the same work, faster*. That is not on offer, because the expensive parts — deciding which account to believe, whether prior practice governs, what conduct amounted to — are the parts you may not delegate. What you get is **recovered minutes**, and the only question is which rung you spend them on.

**Spend them on rung two: corroboration.** Establishing what exists, what the record omits, what conflicts, what is missing. Least visible, first cut under time pressure, where cases are won and lost — and **the rung where AI is genuinely permitted at scale**, because establishing what exists is verifiable by reading the underlying documents. Undirected, the minutes go into closing more matters (improves the metric, does nothing for the product), into better-written reports (**polish is not strength, and it can hide a rung breach clumsy prose would have exposed**), or into the queue, absorbed invisibly.

**The bet: four terms.** The **change**, specific enough to implement without a follow-up question. The **measure with a baseline** — skipping the baseline converts the exercise into an anecdote. The **funding line**: what gets less attention, because *we'll absorb it* means it will not happen. The **kill condition** decided now, with four parts — what you would see, **who is watching for it**, by when, and what happens then.

**And the half people avoid: what would you turn off?** Somebody on your team is likely already using a general-purpose assistant on case content, under exactly this pressure. **For some readers the strongest available bet is not a deployment — it is a sanctioned tool replacing an unsanctioned one, and a conversation that surfaces what is already happening.** A bet that ignores what your team is already doing is a bet on a fiction.
